hyades.name: Hyades
hyades.introduction: is the nearest open cluster, about 150 light-years away in Taurus: hundreds of stars that share the same age, origin and motion through space. Its brightest stars draw the V-shaped face of the Bull. The brighter orange Aldebaran at the tip of the V is not a member; at 65 light-years, it lies far in front of the cluster.

image.alt: The V-shaped Hyades star cluster, with the bright orange foreground star Aldebaran at upper left.
image.caption: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/Digitized Sky Survey 2 · survey composite · released 2020
image.credit: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/Digitized Sky Survey 2. Wide-field composite of Digitized Sky Survey 2 plates, released August 2020. Aldebaran, at upper left, lies in front of the cluster. Resized from the 1280-pixel Commons rendition to 600 × 350 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: The Hyades star cluster (noirlab2018e)

sections.title: The first planet in a cluster
sections.text: Ain, the Bull’s Eye, carries a gas giant planet, the first planet found in any open cluster. Four more Hyades stars are now known to host planets: HD 285507 has a hot Jupiter, K2-25 a Neptune-sized planet, K2-136 a system of three and TOI-4364 a mini-Neptune.

sections.title: Giants at the head of the Bull
sections.text: The five brightest members have used up the hydrogen in their cores and swollen into giants. Four of them, Prima Hyadum, Secunda Hyadum, Ain and Chamukuy, outline the head of Taurus together with Aldebaran. The fifth, Theta1 Tau, sits right next to the brighter Chamukuy, a close pair visible to the naked eye.

sections.title: Weeping sisters
sections.text: In Greek myth the Hyades were five daughters of Atlas and half-sisters of the Pleiades. After their brother Hyas died, the weeping sisters became stars, and the cluster has been linked with rain ever since; in England it was known as the “April Rainers”. Homer’s Iliad already places it on the shield that Hephaistos forged for Achilles. Messier left it out of his 1781 catalog, so it has no Messier number.

sections.title: A rung on the distance ladder
sections.text: The Hyades are close enough to measure directly: as Earth orbits the Sun, the member stars shift back and forth against the distant sky. Hipparcos and Hubble measured that shift, and comparing the stars’ colors and brightness gives the same 47 parsecs. Because the two methods agree, the cluster anchors the ladder of methods that reaches out to other galaxies.

sections.title: Dated by its faintest members
sections.text: Stars destroy their lithium once their cores get hot enough, but the faintest brown dwarfs never do. In 2018, spectra of six brown dwarfs in the Hyades from the 10.4-meter Gran Telescopio Canarias showed lithium only in the two coolest. Where it disappears dates the cluster to 650 ± 70 million years. Until then, the method had only worked for clusters younger than about 200 million years.

source.title: Martín et al. (2018): The lithium depletion boundary and the age of the Hyades cluster

sections.title: Slowly evaporating
sections.text: At birth the Hyades probably held 800–1,600 solar masses of stars, much more than today. Heavier stars sink to the core and fling lighter ones outward, where the Milky Way’s pull strips them away. About a third of the known members already lie beyond the cluster’s tidal radius of 33 light-years. In the end, perhaps a dozen star systems will remain.

pleiades.name: Pleiades
pleiades.introduction: is the star cluster most obvious to the naked eye, about 440 light-years away in Taurus. Also called the Seven Sisters and Messier 45, it holds more than 1,000 stars born together; six or seven of them are easy to see without a telescope, even from light-polluted cities.

image.alt: The bright blue-white stars of the Pleiades in a wide star field, wrapped in faint blue reflection nebulosity.
image.caption: Brody Wesner · telescope photograph · October 2024
image.credit: Brody Wesner. Telescope photograph taken October 9, 2024, with about 13 hours of total exposure. Resized from the 1280-pixel Commons rendition to 600 × 389 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: Pleiades 2024

sections.title: Seven sisters, six stars
sections.text: The brightest stars carry the names of the Seven Sisters of Greek myth, Alcyone, Asterope, Celaeno, Electra, Maia, Merope and Taygeta, and of their parents, Atlas and Pleione. Giovanni Battista Riccioli first recorded these names in 1665. Cultures around the world saw the cluster as seven sisters, and their myths explain why only six of them shine.

sections.title: Older than the calendar
sections.text: Around 2330 BC the Pleiades marked the spring equinox, and many ancient calendars began with them. The Nebra sky disk, made in Germany around 1600 BC, shows the cluster between the Sun and the Moon, likely its earliest known picture. In Japan the cluster is Subaru, “to cluster together”: the name of an 8.2-meter telescope on Mauna Kea and of a carmaker with six stars in its logo.

sections.title: Galileo’s 36 stars
sections.text: Galileo Galilei was the first to turn a telescope on the cluster. His 1610 sketch in Sidereus Nuncius shows 36 stars, far more than the eye can see. In 1767 John Michell calculated that the chance of so many bright stars lining up by accident was 1 in 500,000, so they had to belong together. Charles Messier listed the cluster as M45 in 1771.

sections.title: A distance that would not settle
sections.text: Before the Hipparcos satellite, the Pleiades were thought to be about 135 parsecs away. Hipparcos then measured only 118. Hubble, star-color fits and an orbit of the double star Atlas all pointed back to 133–140 parsecs. Radio interferometry in 2014 found 136.2 parsecs and called the Hipparcos value an error. Gaia’s third data release puts the cluster at 135.74 ± 0.10 parsecs.

sections.title: Dated by its faintest stars
sections.text: Young stars destroy their lithium once their cores grow hot enough, and the lighter the star, the longer that takes. In 1998, Keck spectra showed where lithium vanishes among the cluster’s faintest members, at spectral type M6.5. Compared with models, that boundary dates the Pleiades to 125 ± 8 million years, older than the 75–100 million years most studies had assumed until then.

source.title: Stauffer, Schultz & Kirkpatrick (1998): Keck spectra of Pleiades brown dwarf candidates and a precise determination of the lithium depletion edge in the Pleiades

sections.title: Full of failed stars
sections.text: Brown dwarfs, too light to fuse hydrogen, may make up a quarter of the cluster’s members but less than 2% of its mass. Young brown dwarfs are still warm and bright, so astronomers hunt for them in clusters like this one; in older clusters they have cooled and faded.

sections.title: Borrowed time
sections.text: Like most open clusters, the Pleiades will not stay together. Close encounters fling some stars out, and the Milky Way’s tides strip others away. Encounters with giant molecular clouds and the spiral arms speed this up: in about 250 million years, the cluster will have dispersed.

beehive-cluster.name: Beehive Cluster
beehive-cluster.introduction: is one of the nearest open clusters, about 600 light-years away in Cancer: around 1,000 stars born together that a dark sky shows as a small misty patch. Also called Praesepe, “the manger”, and Messier 44, it shares its age and its path through space with the Hyades.

image.alt: The scattered white and orange stars of the Beehive Cluster against a dark star field.
image.caption: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Burrell Schmidt telescope · January 1997
image.credit: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Approximately true-color composite of fifteen B, V and R images taken in January 1997 with the Burrell Schmidt telescope of Case Western Reserve University on Kitt Peak. Resized from the 1280-pixel Commons rendition to 600 × 600 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: M44, NGC 2632 (noao-m44)

sections.title: Planets around Sun-like stars
sections.text: In September 2012, two hot Jupiters were found in the Beehive Cluster, circling the stars Pr0201 and Pr0211. They were the first planets known to orbit Sun-like stars in a star cluster. In 2016 a second planet turned up around Pr0211, the first system of several planets in an open cluster. Kepler’s K2 mission has since found planets around seven more members; K2-264 has two.

sections.title: Forty stars for Galileo
sections.text: Galileo turned one of his first telescopes on the misty patch and counted 40 stars. Johann Bayer had drawn it in 1603 as a nebulous star named Epsilon, and cited the Arabic name Meleph, “the stall”. Both names now belong to its brightest star, Meleph. Charles Messier added the cluster to his catalog in 1769, perhaps to make his list longer than the 42 objects of his rival Lacaille.

sections.title: A manger, a mist and a ghost
sections.text: Greeks and Romans saw a manger with two donkeys eating from it, the stars Asellus Borealis and Asellus Australis. Both are foreground stars, at less than a third of the cluster’s distance. Hipparchus called the cluster Nephelion, “little cloud”, and Aratus “little mist”. In China it lay in the Ghost lunar mansion, a demon riding in a carriage, and was also known as the “exhalation of piled-up corpses”.

sections.title: A sibling of the Hyades
sections.text: Eleven isochrone ages from the literature put the Beehive Cluster at 670 ± 67 million years. Its Sun-like stars spin slightly faster than their counterparts in the Hyades, by 0.4 days on average, so the Hyades are the older cluster, by about 57 million years: less than the uncertainty of either age. Among the cooler, lighter stars the difference disappears, a sign that these stars stop slowing down for a while.

source.title: Douglas et al. (2019): K2 rotation periods for low-mass Hyads and a quantitative comparison of the distribution of slow rotators in the Hyades and Praesepe

sections.title: Giants, white dwarfs and few brown dwarfs
sections.text: About two thirds of the cluster’s members are red dwarfs. Five stars have already swollen into giants, and eleven white dwarfs are the remains of its heaviest stars, once hot stars of spectral type B. Brown dwarfs are rare, probably because, like other light members, they drifted to the cluster’s outskirts, where the Milky Way’s tides stripped them away.

ngc-869.name: Double Cluster
ngc-869.introduction: is a pair of young open clusters, NGC 869 and NGC 884, about 7,500 light-years away in Perseus. Also known as h and Chi Persei and Caldwell 14, both are visible to the naked eye. They form the core of the Perseus OB1 association of hot young stars in the Perseus Arm of the Milky Way.

image.alt: The two dense star clusters NGC 869 and NGC 884 side by side in a rich star field.
image.caption: Taavi Niittee · astrophotograph · January 2022
image.credit: Taavi Niittee. Astrophotograph dated January 11, 2022, dedicated to the public domain. Resized from the 1280-pixel Commons rendition to 600 × 400 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: Double cluster

sections.title: A cluster still assembling
sections.text: Gaia data published in 2021 show that the Double Cluster is not alone. Within 3° of it, seven clusters move together, h and χ Persei among them and three unknown before, embedded in a halo of stars of about 100,000 solar masses. All share the same age and chemistry. The whole complex, named LISCA I, may be merging into one massive cluster, a way of building clusters that could be common in disk galaxies.

source.title: Dalessandro et al. (2021): First phase space portrait of a hierarchical stellar structure in the Milky Way

sections.title: Only 14 million years old
sections.text: A 2010 survey photographed about 47,000 stars in the field and took spectra of 11,000. The hottest stars about to leave the main sequence, the brightness of the red supergiants and the young stars still contracting toward the main sequence all give the same age: about 14 million years for both clusters and their halo. At least 13,000 stars belong to the region, with a total mass of at least 20,000 Suns.

source.title: Currie et al. (2010): The stellar population of h and χ Persei

sections.title: Red supergiants among blue stars
sections.text: The hottest stars still burning hydrogen in their cores are blue-white, of spectral type B0. Red supergiants shine among them: NGC 884 holds five prominent ones, all variable and all around 8th magnitude: RS Persei, AD Persei, FZ Persei, V403 Persei and V439 Persei.

sections.title: Half the Sun’s iron
sections.text: In 2022, spectra of 27 red supergiants spread across the complex around the Double Cluster showed the same iron content in all of them: half that of the Sun. The stars scatter by only 0.03 dex, far less than the 0.15–0.20 dex typical of stars in the Milky Way’s disk, which supports the idea that they formed together.

source.title: Fanelli et al. (2022): The chemical content of the red supergiant population in the Perseus complex

sections.title: The hilt of Perseus’s sword
sections.text: Hipparchus cataloged the Double Cluster as a patch of light around 130 BC, and in myth it is the jeweled hilt of the hero’s sword. Johann Bayer gave it the letters h and χ in 1603. Messier left it out of his catalog. It never sets from most northern temperate latitudes, lies near the radiant of the Perseid meteor shower and is invisible from south of about 30° S.

messier-67.name: Messier 67
messier-67.introduction: is an old open cluster about 2,700 light-years away in Cancer. Its stars are about four billion years old and close to the Sun in age and chemical makeup, which makes it one of the most studied clusters in the sky. It is also known as NGC 2682, the King Cobra Cluster and the Golden Eye Cluster.

image.alt: The compact star cluster Messier 67, with a few orange giants among its many white stars.
image.caption: Starhopper · astrophotograph · 2011
image.credit: Starhopper. Astrophotograph uploaded to Commons in April 2011. Resized from the 1280-pixel Commons rendition to 600 × 613 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: M067

sections.title: A planet around a solar twin
sections.text: For six years, ESO’s HARPS spectrograph tracked 88 stars in Messier 67 for the wobble that orbiting planets cause. It found three planets. Two are hot Jupiters with about a third of Jupiter’s mass, circling Sun-like stars in seven and five days. One of those hosts is among the closest solar twins known: the first solar twin in a cluster found to have a planet.

source.title: ESO: First planet found around solar twin in star cluster (eso1402)

sections.title: Listening to its giants
sections.text: Stars ring with sound waves that change their brightness very slightly. Using K2 light curves, a 2025 study measured these oscillations in Messier 67’s stars, from subgiants to red giants burning helium in their cores; no other cluster had been studied across that whole sequence. The oscillations weigh each star and date the cluster to 3.95 ± 0.35 billion years.

source.title: Reyes et al. (2025): Asteroseismic study of subgiants and giants of the open cluster M67 using Kepler/K2

sections.title: Spinning like the Sun
sections.text: In 2016, K2 light curves timed the starspots of 20 Sun-like stars in the cluster. These four-billion-year-old stars turn once in about 26 days, just like the Sun, whose equator turns in 25.38 days. It supports a key idea of solar and stellar physics: what holds for the Sun holds for other stars of the same size and age.

sections.title: Not the Sun’s birthplace
sections.text: With its age, its composition and more than 100 stars like the Sun, Messier 67 was once proposed as the cluster the Sun was born in. Computer simulations disagree on whether the outer Solar System could have survived being ejected from it, and the cluster itself would probably not have survived such an event.

sections.title: No hot stars left
sections.text: Johann Gottfried Koehler discovered the cluster in 1779. Its stars hotter than spectral type F have all used up the hydrogen in their cores, apart perhaps from some of its 30 or so blue stragglers, stars that look younger than the rest. Light stars have been flung outward and lost over the eons; the cluster may once have held about ten times its present mass.

ngc-3532.name: NGC 3532
ngc-3532.introduction: is a rich open cluster about 1,500 light-years away in Carina, easy to see with the naked eye from the southern hemisphere. Also called the Wishing Well Cluster and Caldwell 91, it was the first target ever observed by the Hubble Space Telescope.

image.alt: Hundreds of blue-white and orange stars of NGC 3532, with glowing red gas behind them.
image.caption: ESO/G. Beccari · MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope · February 2013
image.credit: ESO/G. Beccari. Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, February 2013. The red gas and dark dust lanes lie in the background and are probably not connected to the cluster. Resized from the 1280-pixel Commons rendition to 480 × 464 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: The colourful star cluster NGC 3532 (eso1439a)

sections.title: From Lacaille to Hubble
sections.text: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille discovered the cluster in 1752 while observing from South Africa. During his stay in southern Africa in the 1830s, John Herschel noted “several elegant double stars” in it. On 20 May 1990 it became the first target observed by the Hubble Space Telescope.

source.title: ESO: A colourful gathering of middle-aged stars (eso1439)

sections.title: Silver coins in a well
sections.text: Its stars look like silver coins dropped into a well, hence the name Wishing Well Cluster. Its oval shape also earned it the name Football Cluster, after a rugby ball. It covers an area of sky almost twice the size of the full Moon.

source.title: ESO: A colourful gathering of middle-aged stars (eso1439)

sections.title: As rich as the Pleiades
sections.text: Radial velocities collected over a decade with telescopes in Australia and Chile, combined with Gaia proper motions, confirmed 660 members, from giants down to red dwarfs. That makes NGC 3532 one of the richest open clusters known, on par with the Pleiades. Model isochrones fitted to these members confirm an age of about 300 million years.

source.title: Fritzewski et al. (2019): Spectroscopic membership for the populous 300 Myr-old open cluster NGC 3532

sections.title: Blue stars and orange giants
sections.text: At 300 million years, NGC 3532 is middle-aged for an open cluster. Its stars of moderate mass still shine blue-white, while the heavier ones have used up their hydrogen and become orange-red giants. Its heaviest stars exploded as supernovae long ago.

source.title: ESO: A colourful gathering of middle-aged stars (eso1439)

sections.title: Heavyweight white dwarfs
sections.text: Four white dwarfs in NGC 3532 have cooling times that span about 90 million years, so they come from stars of different masses. Yet all weigh about 0.9–1 solar mass: above about four solar masses, a heavier star seems to leave a white dwarf only a little heavier.

source.title: Dobbie et al. (2012): Further investigation of white dwarfs in the open clusters NGC 2287 and NGC 3532

omega-centauri.name: Omega Centauri
omega-centauri.introduction: is the largest and most massive globular cluster of the Milky Way, about 17,700 light-years away in Centaurus: some ten million stars packed into a ball. To the naked eye it looks like a fuzzy star, which is why it carries a star’s name. It is also known as NGC 5139.

image.alt: A dense round swarm of countless white and yellow stars, brightest toward the middle.
image.caption: ESO · Wide Field Imager, MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope · 2008
image.credit: ESO. Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla; the central part of the cluster, about the size of the full Moon. Released in 2008. Resized from the 1280-pixel Commons rendition to 480 × 451 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: Omega Centauri by ESO

sections.title: The heart of a swallowed galaxy
sections.text: Most globular clusters formed their stars all at once. Omega Centauri holds stars of many ages and very different metal content, so it is thought to be the core of a dwarf galaxy that the Milky Way tore apart and absorbed. Kapteyn’s Star, now only 13 light-years from the Sun, probably came from the same lost galaxy.

sections.title: Ages star by star
sections.text: In 2024 the oMEGACat survey fitted the ages of more than 8,100 subgiant stars one by one, using Hubble photometry and MUSE spectra. Most formed between 13 and 10 billion years ago, with a mean of 12.08 billion years. The more metal-rich a star, the younger it tends to be, and the stars fall into two distinct streams, hinting that they formed in different ways.

source.title: Clontz et al. 2024: oMEGACat IV, ages of Omega Centauri subgiants

sections.title: A black hole in hiding?
sections.text: In 2008 the motions of stars near the center pointed to a black hole of about 40,000 solar masses. Later studies with a revised center found no sign of it and limited any black hole to 12,000 solar masses. In July 2024 seven unusually fast stars near the core revived the case for a black hole of at least 8,200 solar masses, but that, too, has been questioned.

sections.title: A star that was not one
sections.text: Around the year 150, Ptolemy listed it as a star on the centaur’s back, and in 1603 Johann Bayer gave it the Greek letter omega. Edmond Halley saw in 1677 that it was not a star. In 1826 James Dunlop recognized it as a globular cluster, a “beautiful globe of stars very gradually and moderately compressed to the centre”.

47-tucanae.name: 47 Tucanae
47-tucanae.introduction: is the second-brightest globular cluster in the sky, after Omega Centauri, about 14,700 light-years away in Tucana. Millions of stars crowd toward its small, very bright core, and it hosts dozens of millisecond pulsars. It is also known as NGC 104; in the sky it sits beside the Small Magellanic Cloud, a separate galaxy more than ten times farther away.

image.alt: A bright, dense globular cluster with a brilliant white core, fading into scattered stars at its edges.
image.caption: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · CTIO 4-metre Blanco telescope · 1975
image.credit: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Photographed with the CTIO 4-metre Blanco telescope in 1975. Resized from the 1280-pixel Commons rendition to 600 × 480 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: 47 Tucanae, NGC 104 (noao-02212)

sections.title: A city of pulsars
sections.text: 47 Tucanae holds 35 known millisecond pulsars, more than any cluster but Terzan 5. They were spun up by gas from companion stars. In one system, 47 Tuc W, the companion still seems to pass gas to its pulsar, caught in the change from X-ray binary to millisecond pulsar. Their combined glow made 47 Tucanae the first globular cluster seen in gamma rays.

sections.title: Where are the planets?
sections.text: Hubble watched the crowded core for planets passing in front of their stars. Ten to fifteen should have turned up at the rate seen near the Sun; none did. A later survey of the uncrowded outskirts also came up empty. The likely reason is not crowding but the cluster’s low metal content, too poor to build planets easily.

sections.title: Mistaken for a comet
sections.text: Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille recorded it in 1751–52 from South Africa and first took it for the head of a comet. Its number comes from Johann Elert Bode’s 1801 catalog, which sorted Lacaille’s stars by constellation. Benjamin Gould later named it ξ Tucanae, but the name never caught on.

sections.title: The Bright Star
sections.text: The cluster’s brightest star in visible and ultraviolet light is a blue giant known simply as the “Bright Star”. It shines about 1,100 times as brightly as the Sun with only about half the Sun’s mass: an old star that has already left the asymptotic giant branch and now burns helium.

messier-4.name: Messier 4
messier-4.introduction: is the nearest globular cluster, about 6,000 light-years away in Scorpius, just 1.3° west of Antares. It looks about as large as the full Moon, and it was the first globular cluster in which single stars were resolved. It is also known as NGC 6121.

image.alt: A loose globular cluster of white and orange stars against a rich star field.
image.caption: ESO Imaging Survey · Wide Field Imager, MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope · 2012
image.credit: ESO Imaging Survey. Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, released in September 2012. Resized from the 1280-pixel Commons rendition to 600 × 580 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: Globular star cluster Messier 4

sections.title: A planet from the dawn of the Galaxy
sections.text: Just outside the core, the pulsar PSR B1620-26 circles a white dwarf every 191 days, and a giant planet orbits them both. A team led by Donald Backer noticed in the early 1990s that a third body tugged on the pair, and Stephen Thorsett and colleagues announced in 1993 that it was a planet. Born with the cluster, it is thought to be about 12 billion years old.

source.title: Wikipedia: PSR B1620−26

sections.title: Cooling embers
sections.text: In 1995 Hubble found white dwarfs in Messier 4, the burnt-out cores of Sun-like stars, that rank among the oldest known stars in the Galaxy, about 13 billion years old.

sections.title: Plunging toward the center
sections.text: Messier 4 follows an elongated orbit that takes it within about 2,000 light-years of the Galactic center and out to about 19,000 light-years. Each time it crosses the disk, the Milky Way’s tides shake it and strip stars away, so the cluster was probably once much more massive.

sections.title: Herschel’s bar
sections.text: In 1783 William Herschel noticed a short bar of 11th-magnitude stars across the core, about 2.5′ long, still visible in moderate telescopes. Around it the cluster is rather loosely packed for a globular cluster.

sections.title: Something heavy at the center
sections.text: In 2023 Hubble and Gaia measurements of the stars’ motions revealed about 800 solar masses of unseen matter packed into the very center. It could be a black hole of intermediate mass, or a tight swarm of white dwarfs, neutron stars and small black holes.

messier-13.name: Messier 13
messier-13.introduction: is a globular cluster of several hundred thousand stars about 24,200 light-years away in Hercules, often called the most magnificent globular cluster seen from the north. On dark nights it is just visible to the naked eye in the Keystone of Hercules. It is also known as NGC 6205 and the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules.

image.alt: A round, glowing ball of countless stars, bluish-white at the center.
image.caption: Astrowimp · astrophotograph · 2015
image.credit: Astrowimp. Astrophotograph taken from eastern North Carolina in April 2015. Resized from the 1280-pixel Commons rendition to 600 × 474 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: M13 (Hercules globular cluster)

sections.title: A message to the stars
sections.text: In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a message toward Messier 13, with information about humans, DNA, atomic numbers and Earth’s position. It was a demonstration of technology rather than a real attempt at contact; M13 was simply a large, fairly close cluster in the right part of the sky. The message needs about 25,000 years to arrive, and by then the cluster will have moved.

sections.title: Packed tight enough to collide
sections.text: The stars of Messier 13 are packed more than a hundred times more densely than those around the Sun. They sometimes collide and merge into “blue stragglers”, stars that look younger than their neighbors. Like other old clusters, M13 is poor in metals: it has only about 4.6% of the Sun’s share of iron.

sections.title: Halley’s find
sections.text: Edmond Halley discovered the cluster in 1714, and Charles Messier added it to his catalog on 1 June 1764. Single stars in it were first resolved in 1779. A photograph of M13 decorates the dome of St Anne’s Church in Kew, London, dedicated in 1714, the year of Halley’s discovery.

sections.title: A home for fictional empires
sections.text: Messier 13 is a favorite of science fiction. Isaac Asimov’s “Sucker Bait” and Poul Anderson’s Question and Answer take place on a world inside it, the Perry Rhodan series puts the Arkonide homeworld Arkon there, and Kurt Vonnegut’s The Sirens of Titan counts the miles the Solar System gains toward it every hour.

messier-22.name: Messier 22
messier-22.introduction: is one of the nearest globular clusters, about 10,800 light-years away in Sagittarius, near the Teapot asterism. It is the brightest globular cluster visible from mid-northern latitudes, though it stays low in their southern sky. It is also known as NGC 6656 and the Great Sagittarius Cluster.

image.alt: A dense field of white, yellow and orange stars filling the frame.
image.caption: ESA/Hubble & NASA · Hubble · 2015
image.credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA. The center of the cluster seen by Hubble, released in April 2015. Resized from the 1280-pixel Commons rendition to 480 × 490 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: The crammed centre of Messier 22

sections.title: Black holes that stayed
sections.text: In 2012 the Very Large Array found two black holes of 10–20 solar masses each in Messier 22, confirmed with the Chandra X-ray telescope. Clusters were thought to fling out their black holes; the find suggests that M22 may still hold 5 to 100 of them, which could explain its unusually large core.

sections.title: A dying star inside
sections.text: Messier 22 is one of only four globular clusters of the Milky Way known to contain a planetary nebula. The IRAS satellite first spotted it as a point of infrared light in 1986, and its nature was found in 1989. Known as GJJC1, it was blown off by a dying star perhaps only 6,000 years ago.

sections.title: A lens on the bulge
sections.text: Messier 22 lies in front of part of the Galactic bulge. When one of its stars passes in front of a distant bulge star, its gravity bends and briefly brightens the light behind it, a microlensing event. This makes the cluster useful for studying such events.

sections.title: One of the first
sections.text: Abraham Ihle discovered Messier 22 in 1665, making it one of the first globular clusters found. Harlow Shapley studied it in 1930 and counted roughly 70,000 stars. Its red giants show a wide spread of colors, like those of Omega Centauri, which has made it a target of close study since 1977.

messier-15.name: Messier 15
messier-15.introduction: is one of the densest globular clusters in the Milky Way, about 34,900 light-years away in Pegasus. Its core has collapsed into a sharp central spike of stars. It is also known as NGC 7078 and the Great Pegasus Cluster.

image.alt: A dense globular cluster with a brilliant core of blue-white and orange stars.
image.caption: ESA/Hubble & NASA · Hubble · 2011

sections.title: A nebula inside a cluster
sections.text: In 1928 Francis G. Pease found a planetary nebula inside Messier 15, the first known in any globular cluster. Now called Pease 1, it shines at only magnitude 15.5 and needs a telescope of at least 30 cm to be seen. Only a handful have been found in globular clusters since.

source.title: Wikipedia: Pease 1

sections.title: A collapsed core
sections.text: Messier 15 is one of the most densely packed globular clusters known. Its core has contracted in what astronomers call a “core collapse”, leaving a sharp central cusp: an enormous number of stars crowded around what may be a central black hole.

sections.title: Pulsars and X-rays
sections.text: Messier 15 holds 112 known variable stars and 8 pulsars, among them M15-C, a pair of neutron stars. Satellites from Uhuru to Chandra have found two bright X-ray sources in the cluster, M15 X-1 and X-2; X-1 appears to be the first X-ray source discovered in Pegasus.

terzan-5.name: Terzan 5
terzan-5.introduction: is a dense ball of stars near the center of the Milky Way, about 21,600 light-years away in Sagittarius, hidden behind thick dust. Long classed as a globular cluster, it formed stars in several bursts over billions of years and is now seen as a fossil fragment of the Galaxy’s young bulge. It holds more millisecond pulsars than any other cluster.

sections.title: Four generations of stars
sections.text: A globular cluster usually has one ancient population of stars. In 2009 Terzan 5 was found to have two, and in 2016 Hubble dated them to about 12 and 5 billion years. In 2026, Webb and Hubble together refined these to 12.5 and 4.7 billion years and found two more generations, 3.8 and 2.5 billion years old.

source.title: ESA/Webb: Webb and Hubble reveal history of relic of the Milky Way galaxy’s formation (weic2611)

sections.title: A fossil of the bulge
sections.text: To form four generations, Terzan 5 must once have been massive enough to keep the metals that its supernovae forged. It is probably the remnant of one of the giant clumps that merged into the Milky Way’s bulge 12.5 billion years ago and never mixed in. Astronomers now call it a bulge fossil fragment; Liller 1 is the only other known.

source.title: ESA/Webb: Webb and Hubble reveal history of relic of the Milky Way galaxy’s formation (weic2611)

sections.title: The fastest-spinning star
sections.text: Terzan 5 holds 49 known millisecond pulsars, as of December 2023, and perhaps as many as 200. Among them is PSR J1748−2446ad, the fastest-spinning pulsar known: it turns 716 times every second. Its crowded core makes stars meet often and form close pairs, including neutron stars with companions, which explains its many pulsars and X-ray sources.

sections.title: Hidden behind dust
sections.text: Agop Terzan discovered it in 1968, first labeling it Terzan 11. It lies in a crowded region of the bulge, heavily obscured by dust, so it is studied mostly in infrared light. Its core is only about 0.5 parsec across, yet it is one of the densest places in the Galaxy.
